hints: Start from the equilibrium expression for a weak acid, $K_a = [H^+][CN^-]/[HCN]$, and think what simplifying assumption you can make about $[H^+]$ and $[CN^-]$ for a very weakly dissociated acid.
Recall how $[H^+]$ is linked to the starting concentration $c$ by $[H^+] = \sqrt{K_a \times c}$, then convert to pH with $pH = -\log[H^+] $.
walkthrough:
Set up the weak acid approximation**
For $\text{HCN(aq)} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+\text{(aq)} + \text{CN}^-\text{(aq)}$, every molecule that dissociates gives one $\text{H}^+$ and one $\text{CN}^-$. Because $K_a$ is tiny, dissociation is tiny, so $[\text{H}^+] \approx [\text{CN}^-]$ and equilibrium $[\text{HCN}] \approx$ initial concentration $0.10 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$. That turns $K_a = [\text{H}^+]^2/c$ into $[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_a \times c}$.

Substitute and convert to pH**
Put the numbers in: $$[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{(6.2 \times 10^{-10})(0.10)} = \sqrt{6.2 \times 10^{-11}} = 7.9 \times 10^{-6} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$ Then: $$pH = -\log[\text{H}^+] = -\log(7.9 \times 10^{-6}) = 5.10$$ A pH just above 5 makes sense for a very weak acid at $0.10 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.

Final answer: $[H^+] = \sqrt{K_a \times c} = \sqrt{6.2 \times 10^{-10} \times 0.10} = 7.9 \times 10^{-6} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$
$pH = -\log(7.9 \times 10^{-6}) = 5.10$

hints: Count outer shell electrons first: H brings 1, C brings 4, N brings 5, total 10, and remember H can only form one bond while C and N need to complete their octets.
walkthrough:
Build H-C triple N from electron counting**
Think of the skeleton as $\text{H}-\text{C}-\text{N}$. H shares its 1 electron with one from C to make a single bond. That leaves C with 3 electrons and N with 5 electrons to share. To give both C and N a full octet, they must share three pairs between them, a triple bond. N keeps its remaining 2 electrons as a lone pair. In your diagram use dots for one atom and crosses for the other, showing 2 electrons in the H-C bond, 6 electrons in the C-N bond, plus 2 non bonding electrons on N.

Final answer: Dot-and-cross diagram showing $\text{H}-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$: single shared pair between H and C, triple shared pair (6 electrons) between C and N, and one lone pair on N. Outer shells only, with H having 2 electrons and C and N each having 8.

hints: Look at the number of sigma bonds plus lone pairs around C and around N in $\text{H}-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ to find the number of electron domains.
Recall what hybridisation and bond angle correspond to two electron domains with no bent shape, as in ethyne.
walkthrough:
Count sigma domains to assign hybridisation**
Focus on sigma bonds plus lone pairs, pi bonds do not create a new direction. C has two sigma bonds, one to H and one to N, with no lone pair, so two domains. N has one sigma bond to C plus one lone pair, so also two domains. Two domains means two hybrid orbitals, which is sp hybridisation for both atoms.

Link sp to linear geometry**
Two sp orbitals point opposite each other to minimise repulsion. The two p orbitals left on each atom then overlap sideways to make the two pi bonds of the triple bond. That leaves a perfectly straight molecule, so the $\text{H}-\text{C}-\text{N}$ angle is $180^{\circ}$.

Final answer: hybridisation of C: sp
hybridisation of N: sp
H-C-N bond angle: $180^{\circ}$

hints: Recall the two classic reactions of alkyl nitriles, $\text{RCN}$: addition of hydrogen gives what class of nitrogen compound, and boiling with aqueous acid gives what class of oxygen compound.
Now replace R with H: reduction adds four H atoms across the triple bond, while full hydrolysis adds water across the triple bond to give a $\text{C=O}$ plus $\text{OH}$ group.
walkthrough:
Reduction to the amine**
Nitriles are reduced by $\text{H}_2$ with Ni catalyst to primary amines: $\text{RCN} + 2\text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{RCH}_2\text{NH}_2$. Here the nitrile carbon already has H attached, so $\text{HCN} + 2\text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$. The triple $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ becomes $\text{C}-\text{N}$ single bonds with extra H atoms added.

Acid hydrolysis to the carboxylic acid**
Heating a nitrile with aqueous $\text{HCl}$ hydrolyses it fully: $\text{RCN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{RCO}_2\text{H} + \text{NH}_3$ (ammonia is protonated to $\text{NH}_4^+$ in acid). With $\text{R} = \text{H}$, the product is $\text{HCO}_2\text{H}$, methanoic acid.

Final answer: A is $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ (methylamine)
B is $\text{HCO}_2\text{H}$ (methanoic acid, formic acid)

hints: Add up the known charges inside the brackets: Ni is +2 from $\text{NiCl}_2$, each $\text{CN}^-$ is 1 minus and each $\text{Cl}^-$ is 1 minus.
walkthrough:
Sum charges to find the overall ion charge**
Ni is in oxidation state +2. Ligands: $2 \times (\text{CN}^-) = 2-$ and $2 \times (\text{Cl}^-) = 2-$. Total: $$(+2) + (-2) + (-2) = -2$$ So the complex ion carries a 2 minus charge.
Final answer: $x = 2-$ i.e. $[\text{Ni(CN)}_2\text{Cl}_2]^{2-}$

hints: Think about isomers that differ only by whether identical ligands are next to each other or opposite each other in a square planar arrangement.
walkthrough:
Recognise cis trans swapping**
With the same square planar shape, you can place the two $\text{CN}^-$ ligands adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans), and similarly for the two $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands. Same formula and bonds, different spatial arrangement, which is the definition of geometrical or cis-trans isomerism.
Final answer: geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism

hints: Use the clue from (b)(ii): the geometry is square planar, so draw Ni at the centre with four positions at the corners of a square.
Remember $\text{CN}^-$ is ambidentate and can bond through C as cyano ($\text{Ni-CN}$) or through N as isocyano ($\text{Ni-NC}$), which creates an extra type of isomerism beyond cis-trans.
Consider how combining cis-trans positions of Cl and Br with C-bonded versus N-bonded cyanide gives two distinct structures that cannot be superimposed.
walkthrough:
Fix the shape as square planar**
Four coordinate Ni(II) with strong field cyanide is square planar. Picture Ni in the middle of a square with ligand positions top left, top right, bottom left, bottom right. Any tetrahedral drawing loses the mark.

Bring in linkage isomerism of cyanide**
Cyanide can donate through carbon to give $\text{Ni-CN}$ or through nitrogen to give $\text{Ni-NC}$. In $[\text{Ni(CN)}_2\text{ClBr}]^{x}$ the Cl and Br are different, so cis-trans alone would give more possibilities, but the observed pair differ by linkage. One isomer has two $\text{Ni-CN}$ groups arranged so Br is trans to a CN and Cl is trans to the other CN.

Draw the second distinct isomer**
The second isomer swaps one cyanide to N-bonded and rearranges positions so Br is trans to Cl while the C-bonded $\text{CN}$ is trans to the N-bonded $\text{NC}$. These two cannot be interconverted by rotation and represent the two structures required.

Final answer: number of isomers = 2
Isomer 1 (square planar): Ni centre with Br trans to C-bonded CN and Cl trans to C-bonded CN, i.e. both cyanides bonded via C.
Isomer 2 (square planar): Ni centre with Br trans to Cl and C-bonded CN trans to N-bonded NC, i.e. one cyano and one isocyano ligand. Both must be clearly square planar.

hints: Start with C: Ni stays +2, sulfate is displaced and no K is present, so C must be a neutral nickel cyanide precipitate, work out the formula that balances $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ with $\text{CN}^-$.
For D and E, use the given K:Ni ratios (2:1 and 3:1) and the fact that Ni remains +2 to work out how many $\text{CN}^-$ ligands are needed to balance the potassium ions.
Think of the sequence as increasing coordination: precipitate, then 4-coordinate tetracyanonickelate(II), then 5-coordinate pentacyanonickelate in excess cyanide.
walkthrough:
Identify C as the simple cyanide precipitate**
$\text{NiSO}_4$ provides $\text{Ni}^{2+}$. Adding $\text{CN}^-$ first precipitates nickel(II) cyanide, with no $\text{K}^+$ and no sulfur included. To neutralise $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ you need two $\text{CN}^-$ ions: $$\text{Ni}^{2+} + 2\text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{Ni(CN)}_2$$ This green precipitate is C.

Form the tetracyano complex D**
With more $\text{KCN}$, the precipitate redissolves as extra $\text{CN}^-$ ligands coordinate: $\text{Ni(CN)}_2 + 2\text{CN}^- \rightarrow [\text{Ni(CN)}_4]^{2-}$. The 2 minus charge needs two $\text{K}^+$ counter ions to give a neutral salt, matching the given K:Ni ratio of 2:1. So D is $\text{K}_2\text{Ni(CN)}_4$, the yellow solution.

Form the pentacyano complex E in excess**
In large excess of $\text{CN}^-$, a fifth ligand adds: $[\text{Ni(CN)}_4]^{2-} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow [\text{Ni(CN)}_5]^{3-}$. The 3 minus charge needs three $\text{K}^+$ ions, matching the K:Ni ratio of 3:1. So E is $\text{K}_3\text{Ni(CN)}_5$, the red solution. Nickel stays +2 throughout.

Final answer: C is $\text{Ni(CN)}_2$
D is $\text{K}_2\text{Ni(CN)}_4$
E is $\text{K}_3\text{Ni(CN)}_5$
